metadata.title: Nahual . creative studio
metadata.description: Turning your vision into digital reality

home.heroText: Among the Nahua, a Mesoamerican people, the deer (Mazātl) is the seventh day of the sacred calendar: a messenger between worlds, associated with grace, vigilance, and the ability to hide its true nature from others. The nahual is the same idea: a human essence revealed in its true animal form, embodied here by this deer.
home.aboutText:
Nahual, the studio, applies the same logic to the web: turning an idea into a real, working site. The proof it worked? It works for everyone.

Sylvain Maurier, senior frontend developer, 10 years of experience (React, Next.js, Vue/Nuxt, React Native). Specialized in digital accessibility (RGAA/WCAG), with one simple conviction: accessibility is built, not just audited.

chapters.line: He grazes in the half-light, indifferent to the path leading toward him.
The stag has noticed you. He doesn't flee — he waits.
A silence. Three entities: your body, his body, what passes between them.
Four directions around you, a fifth at the center. Yours to choose.

projets.title: Projects
projets.intro: Three recent projects. Deep case studies rather than a screenshot gallery.

nuada.title: Nuada · RGAA accessibility audit
nuada.text: Showcase site and RGAA audit engine. WCAG 2.2 compliance, multilingual SEO, positioned as "the auditor who codes the fix."
nuada.context: The French RGAA audit market is saturated with PDF reports no one knows how to implement. Nuada was built around a simple idea: deliver the fix code, not just the diagnosis.
nuada.role: Product owner, art direction, complete development. Solo builder.
nuada.stack: Astro, TypeScript, MDX, native i18n fr/en/es, Netlify hosting.
nuada.highlights: Rare positioning against classic firms ("the auditor who codes"). Public transparent pricing grid. Quick online audit demo on submitted URL.
nuada.outcome: Live since August 2026. First conversations with 3 prospects between September and October.

detail.hero: The auditor who codes the fix.

narrative.title: The market reality
narrative.text: The French RGAA accessibility audit market is mature but paradoxical. Large firms deliver 80-page PDF reports, structured against the 106 criteria of the standard, listing each non-compliance with a screenshot and a generic recommendation. The engineering teams receiving those reports are often left helpless: how do you translate "improve link focus contrast" into a concrete pull request? Nuada starts from that observation to propose something else.

narrative.title: The technical stance
narrative.text: Each non-compliance identified by Nuada is delivered with directly implementable fix code, tested on a client project fork when possible. No vague "recommendation," no "to investigate on the team side": a Git diff, an explanation of why, a non-regression test. The auditor becomes a temporary contributor, not a consultant leaving behind a knot of problems.

narrative.title: Site architecture
narrative.text: Astro for static generation, native i18n for fr/en/es with no overhead, MDX for long-form articles, Netlify hosting with preview branches for each new piece of content. The site itself is RGAA 4.1 compliant by construction — no post-audit patching, every component is designed accessible from the start. A test-driven a11y approach that serves as its own example.

narrative.title: What Nuada teaches me
narrative.text: Building Nuada forced me to formalize what was implicit: what I did intuitively on client missions (deliver code rather than text) becomes a reproducible method. The real deliverable of an accessibility audit isn't a document, it's a codebase more accessible than before.

narrative.title: Next steps
narrative.text: Once the RGAA certification is validated (access42 exam October 23, 2026), Nuada can move from showcase site to real tool: partial audit automation via axe-core in CI, before/after comparator on pull request, public library of reusable accessible patterns.

kleyfrance.title: KleyFrance
kleyfrance.text: Full WordPress site rebuild + logo creation for a manufacturer of custom lifting solutions (oil, offshore, military).
kleyfrance.context: Aging site, not responsive, no visual charter. International B2B target with demanding, very technical vocabulary (slinging, marine winches, LOLER).
kleyfrance.role: Art direction, logo creation, WordPress custom theme rebuild.
kleyfrance.stack: WordPress, ACF Pro, responsive custom theme, subtle GSAP animations.
kleyfrance.highlights: Industrial visual charter without falling into "heavy metal" cliché. Product photothèque organized by sector (naval / offshore / defense). B2B multilingual SEO.
kleyfrance.outcome: Site live, loading time cut by 3, mobile-friendly, unified quote forms.

detail.hero: Making a niche industrial site breathe.

narrative.title: Client context
narrative.text: KleyFrance is a French manufacturer of custom lifting solutions — slings, winches, specialized spreader beams — for very specialized sectors: oil, offshore oceanography, military industry. A legacy WordPress site, not responsive, whose graphic charter came down to an aging logo and a gray-blue palette without identity. The brief: rebuild while keeping industrial credibility, without falling into the "heavy metal" cliché that plagues this market.

narrative.title: Art direction approach
narrative.text: Rather than a flashy site, a design that breathes technical seriousness. Product photos on a clean background, sober but modern industrial typography (not thick futura, rather a balanced neo-grotesque), tight palette deep blue + functional orange like a safety marking ribbon. The redesigned logo keeps the founder's "K" spirit but with golden ratio proportions, legible at 16px as at 2m on a trade show.

narrative.title: The editorial challenge
narrative.text: The vocabulary is ultra-specialized. "Balancing spreader beam," "30t hydraulic underwater winch," "DNV/LOLER compliance." The site had to remain accessible to technical buyers (who know) without scaring off more generalist buyers (military, industrialists). Solution: a systematic dual reading — an explicit title in plain French, a precise technical subtitle with the industry vocabulary.

narrative.title: Concrete impact
narrative.text: Loading time divided by 3 (optimized WordPress, WebP images, Cloudflare cache). Mobile-first responsive. Unified quote forms with pre-filled conditions by target sector. Client feedback: incoming first contacts become more qualified — prospects arrive having understood the specialization before contacting.

narrative.title: What I take from it
narrative.text: In a B2B niche market, art direction matters more than one might think. Technical credibility comes through graphic choices consistent with the trade — no unnecessary creative dev effects, but each element must signal "we know what we're talking about."

synapse.title: Synapse
synapse.text: Open-source plugin for Claude Code: syncs an AI assistant's memory across machines and projects instead of duplicating it.
synapse.context: Using Claude Code on 3 machines (personal, LR mission, laptop), I kept losing continuity: each machine had its own memory, none knew the others' context. Time-consuming and fragile manual duplication.
synapse.role: Concept, architecture, complete dev, tests, docs, publication. Solo.
synapse.stack: Node.js, TypeScript, Claude Code hooks, background git sync, smart local cache.
synapse.highlights: Sync collision detection (two machines writing at the same time). Named memory structure (feedback/project/user/reference). 283 tests, green CI from day 1. Published open-source from day 1.
synapse.outcome: Published on github.com/smaurier/claude-synapse. Plugin adopted daily on my 3 machines. Solid base for a future community.

detail.hero: A continuous AI memory across three machines.

narrative.title: The lived problem
narrative.text: In 2026, I use Claude Code daily on three machines: my personal setup at home, the one on mission at LR Technologies, a backup laptop. Each machine manages its own memory (user preferences, project context, validated feedback). Result: I repeat the same explanations to Claude on each machine, or worse, I manually copy memory files between machines with conflict risks. The "multiple assistants that don't know each other" pattern quickly becomes counterproductive.

narrative.title: Architecture chosen
narrative.text: Synapse is a plugin that bootstraps a Git-versioned memory structure, with automatic background sync on every significant change. Memory is typed: feedback (learned work rules), project (active project context), user (user profile), reference (pointers to external sources). Each entry has explicit YAML frontmatter, a short description, a type. A `[[name]]` linking system weaves entries together like a mini knowledge graph.

narrative.title: Technical choices
narrative.text: Node.js + TypeScript for cross-platform. Native Claude Code hooks (SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit) to intercept key moments without monkey-patching. Background Git sync via non-blocking `child_process`. Smart local cache to avoid unnecessary network round-trips. Sync collision detection: two machines write at the same time, Synapse attempts automatic per-entry merge, alerts the user on conflict.

narrative.title: Quality as obligation
narrative.text: 283 tests from the first public release, green CI, coverage > 80%. Why this rigor for a personal plugin? Because memory is precious — a bug that silently overwrites an entry is context lost that I won't recover. TDD here isn't dogma but a guarantee that memory doesn't corrupt itself.

narrative.title: Community opening
narrative.text: Published open-source from the first commit on github.com/smaurier/claude-synapse. Careful documentation, concrete examples, ADR (Architecture Decision Records) to trace choices. Ambition: that other multi-machine Claude Code users can bootstrap their own system. No business model, no premium — a tool solving a real problem for those who have it.

contact.title: Contact

memoire.title: Teyolía · Memory
memoire.intro: Teyolía, one of the three entities that, in Nahua thought, make up a person: it lives in the heart, carries memory, and it's the one that travels to Mictlán after death. This page isn't a blog: it's an epitaph. What didn't survive building this site, kept rather than erased.

entries.title: The walk
entries.text: The stag advanced with the scroll, a technically correct stride cycle, unreadable over the few notches of a real scroll. Removed rather than tuned a third time: it added almost nothing for what it cost.

entries.title: The tree that wasn't from here
entries.text: A first accent of flora, photoreal texture, oversized, clashed with the rest of the scene, flat and vertex-colored. Replaced by a procedural ocotillo, truer to the pre-Columbian flora of central Mexico.

entries.title: The serpents
entries.text: Two attempts at a Xiuhcoatl for the loading veil, two admitted failures: a polyline too thin with no recognizable head, then a still-flawed trace. Removed while waiting for a real hand-drawn silhouette instead of one more procedural pass.

entries.title: The intro that dissolved
entries.text: The Piedra del Sol and the text dissolved into a cloud of embers before revealing the scene. A real vector technique (sampling around 250 SVG paths), but the effect didn't serve the story. Removed the day after it shipped.

entries.title: The calendar glyphs
entries.text: Five hybrid glyphs — Nahui Ollin for Center, Tonatiuh for East, Xochitl for South, Iztli for West, Ollin for North — drawn to animate cardinal transitions. Technically successful, but their codex fidelity made them sacred. Removed without regret, out of respect.

entries.title: The 2D petal curtain
entries.text: First attempt at inter-page transition: 1800 solid ellipses in mix-blend screen crossing the screen like confetti. Fast to code, cheap to watch. Replaced by native View Transitions API, more elegant.

entries.title: The slicing blade
entries.text: An HTML overlay that cut the screen into horizontal slices and slid them in the cardinal direction, like unfolding origami. Too mechanical, too readable as an effect, not organic enough for the site's cosmology.

entries.title: The 3D petal storm
entries.text: A rain of Three.js particles ejected from the stag during transition. Strong signal but confused reading: no clear focal point. Duplicated the existing petals' dispersion. Removed when View Transitions API took over.

entries.title: The brutal fade
entries.text: First iteration of transitions: router.push without burst, sharp WebGL canvas cut, next page appearing instantly. Technically correct, narratively disastrous. The stag teleported between worlds instead of crossing them.

entries.title: The sticky cursor
entries.text: First custom cursor attempt: lerp 0.02, a ring that took two seconds to catch up with the mouse. "Chewing gum" feel. Fixed to 0.15 to let the trail breathe without gluing it.

entries.title: The axial jade flame
entries.text: First Center Xiuhtecuhtli: a three-meter fire column crossing the stag. Strong signature, but it blinded the subject. Reduced to modest embers rising in a circle rather than a single dominant axis.

entries.title: The photorealistic god-rays
entries.text: First East Tonatiuh: GodRaysEffect post-processing shader with full volumetric sampling. Gorgeous at 60fps on dedicated GPU, catastrophic on mobile (30fps). Replaced with additive triangular planes, mesh-based, free to render.

memoire.creditNote: The cardinal motifs on this site (sun, flower, blade, spiral, quincunx) are stylized evocations inspired by Mesoamerican iconography, not reproductions of sacred glyphs. A family tribute to the living Nahua culture, for Elda and our daughters.

codex.title: Codex
codex.intro: A short manual for this site. The cosmogony that structures it, the human who writes it, the family that inhabits it.

cosmos.title: The five directions
cosmos.text: In Mesoamerican thought, the universe isn't read in four cardinal points but in five — the four horizons plus the center. Each direction carries its color, its god, its animal, its time of day. This site follows that plan.

directions.name: Center · Xiuhtecuhtli · jade
directions.text: The cosmic axis, the fire that burns without ever going out. Here is the home, the hub, the possible return.

directions.name: East · Tonatiuh · gold
directions.text: Dawn, the rising sun. Here are the services, what I offer to build with you.

directions.name: South · Huitzilopochtli · turquoise
directions.text: Noon, the warrior hummingbird. Here are the projects, what I've already carried through.

directions.name: West · Ehecatl · ash
directions.text: Dusk, the breath of wind. Here is contact, an open channel.

directions.name: North · Mictlantecuhtli · obsidian
directions.text: Night, the lord of the land of the dead. Here is Teyolía · Memory, what was kept rather than erased.

totem.title: The stag, Mazātl
totem.text: The nahual is that essence which reveals itself in its true animal form. I chose the stag over the eagle or the jaguar — deliberately avoiding the "Aztec imagery" cliché to stay in the more discreet register of presence: messenger between worlds, associated with grace, vigilance, and the ability to hide one's true nature from others.

human.title: Who writes
human.text: Sylvain Maurier, senior frontend developer based in Lyon. Ten years shipping interfaces (React, Next.js, Vue, React Native), an ongoing specialization in digital accessibility (RGAA, certification exam October 23, 2026). A simple thread: accessibility is coded, not just audited. PDF reports don't change the world, fix code does.

family.title: The family that inhabits this site
family.text: Nahual is a French-Mexican project as much as a personal one. Elda, my partner, is Mexican, a native Spanish speaker, a teacher. Léopoldine is our daughter, born in Lyon. Alondra is her older sister, adopted in Mexico. Nahua cosmogony isn't a randomly chosen exotic backdrop — it's a family heritage I'm still learning, with the respect that requires.

respect.title: On cultural appropriation
respect.text: This site pays tribute to a living culture, not a museum. The cardinal motifs (sun, flower, blade, spiral, quincunx) are stylized evocations inspired by Mesoamerican iconography, not reproductions of sacred glyphs. Calendar glyphs, the Fejérváry-Mayer codex, the Piedra del Sol are deliberately absent from decorative elements without context. The red line is simple: celebrate what is public, leave what is sacred to those who hold it.

refs.title: What inspired me
refs.text: Sacred Labs and Joseph Santamaria for WebGL sobriety, Lusion and Immersive Garden for web cinematography, Bruno Simon for the narrative daring of a 3D portfolio. The Fejérváry-Mayer and Borgia codices for the cosmological structure. Miguel León-Portilla's and Alfredo López Austin's studies for the depth of Nahua philosophy. Thanks to Elda for the patience, to Léo for the micro-naps that saved a few deadlines.

accessibilite.title: Accessibility statement
accessibilite.intro: Nahual is committed to making its site accessible under the French General Accessibility Improvement Reference (RGAA) version 4.1.

sections.title: Conformance state
sections.text: This site is partially compliant with RGAA 4.1. A full audit is planned after the 2026 redesign stabilizes.

sections.title: Non-accessible content
sections.text: The interactive 3D scene (WebGL canvas) is decorative: main textual content (titles, texts, links) is accessible to assistive technologies. prefers-reduced-motion is respected.

sections.title: Statement drafting
sections.text: This statement was drafted on August 28, 2026 based on self-assessment. An external audit is planned after obtaining RGAA certification (October 2026).

sections.title: Feedback and contact
sections.text: To report an access issue or obtain an alternative version of content, contact bonjour@nahual.fr. If no response within 60 days, contact the French Rights Defender: https://www.defenseurdesdroits.fr.

confidentialite.title: Privacy policy
confidentialite.intro: This site complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the French Data Protection Act.

sections.title: Data collected
sections.text: No data is collected without your explicit action. Sending a message via the email shown on the Contact page is the only entry point: the information provided (email, message content) is used solely to reply.

sections.title: Cookies and trackers
sections.text: This site does not use tracking cookies or third-party analytics tools (no Google Analytics, no Meta Pixel). Only local storage (localStorage) is used to remember your sound preference (on/off) and whether you've already seen certain animations. This data stays in your browser and is never transmitted.

sections.title: Retention
sections.text: Messages received by email are kept for the time needed to process them, then archived in the responsible party's personal mailbox for future reference. You can request their deletion at any time.

sections.title: Your rights
sections.text: Under GDPR, you have the right to access, rectify, erase, and port your data. Contact: bonjour@nahual.fr.

credits.title: Credits and attributions
credits.intro: This site uses resources created by others. Recognition and gratitude.

sections.title: 3D models
sections.text: The stag and part of the flora come from Quaternius open-source packs (CC0 license). Complementary models (ocotillo, vines, flowers) are procedurally generated.

sections.title: Inspirations

sections.title: Cultural recognition
sections.text: This site is a tribute to the living Nahua culture, not a museum. For Elda, Alondra, Léopoldine, and all who carry this memory.
